newsitem.title: FRANCE: France recalls envoy, warns Iran against violence.
newsitem.headline: France recalls envoy, warns Iran against violence.

text.p: France told Iran on Friday to avoid any violent backlash against German or European interests in Tehran after a German court said Tehran's rulers ordered the murder of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.
Paris joined its 14 European Union partners in recalling its ambassador for "joint consultations about the future of relations between the EU and Iran" after Thursday's verdict.

"In the immediate future, France is particularly attentive to the measures which Iran takes to prevent any inappropriate reaction towards German or European nationals or interests," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
"France's solidarity with Germany is total in this matter," he said.

The 15 EU member states, supporting Germany, decided to recall their ambassadors and said they saw no room to continue their so-called "critical dialogue" while Iran "flouts international norms and indulges in acts of terrorism".

Rummelhardt said the implication of senior state leaders in the case was unacceptable and the EU-Iran dialogue was only possible if Tehran made "a deliberate choice to fit into the international community".
French officials said EU states had not discussed taking economic sanctions against Iran but foreign ministers would review ties with Tehran at a meeting on April 29 in Luxembourg.
Rummelhardt told a briefing that France did not consider the issue at stake to be economic or financial, suggesting the EU was not about to follow a United States call for sanctions against Tehran.
He noted that the United States was by far Iran's biggest foreign trade customer, while France was in fifth place behind Germany, Italy and Britain.
"Iran is a secondary trade partner for France," he said.

Paris imported goods worth a little more than six billion francs ($1 billion) last year -- 95 percent of which was oil and five percent pistachio nuts and rugs -- and sold goods worth three billion francs to Tehran.
The United States has warned French oil companies they could fall foul of controversial American legislation punishing firms that supply oil-drilling equipment to Tehran.
France's Total and Elf Aquitaine are at the top of the list of potential targets of a series of sanctions included in the so-called D'Amato act, named after Republican senator Alfonse d'Amato.
The French government announced plans last month to enact countervailing legislation making it an offence for any French company to comply with such a foreign restriction.
